title: Your toolbox: code, libraries, notebooks and hardware
hook: What people actually use to build AI, and when a simple option is enough.
inPlainWords: You do not build everything from scratch. Most AI work uses a small set of ready-made tools. Tool names change quickly, so learn the roles: a language to write in, libraries that do the heavy lifting, a place to experiment, hardware to run on, and somewhere to keep your work. Check current documentation for the tools of the day.

useCase.title: A two-person team sets up to build ShopEase's first models
useCase.story: The team has a laptop each, a small budget, and no ML infrastructure. They must explore data, train a return-risk model, try a language-model feature, and share their work. What should they set up first?

approaches.name: Spreadsheets and no-code tools
approaches.what: Point-and-click tools with charts and built-in models.
approaches.greatWhen: Quick exploration, non-programmers, and simple tasks.
approaches.avoidWhen: You need control, scale or repeatability.
approaches.example: A spreadsheet chart of returns by category.

approaches.name: Python with notebooks
approaches.what: A programming language plus interactive notebooks for exploring and explaining.
approaches.greatWhen: Exploring data and trying ideas fast.
approaches.avoidWhen: As the only place production code lives.
approaches.example: Load the orders table and plot return rates.

approaches.name: Libraries for classic ML
approaches.what: Ready-made toolkits for tables: cleaning, models and scoring.
approaches.avoidWhen: Images or text at large scale.
approaches.example: Train a boosted-tree model in a few lines.

approaches.name: Libraries for deep learning
approaches.what: Frameworks that train neural networks, usually on GPUs.

approaches.name: Hubs of pretrained models
approaches.what: Public libraries of models and datasets you can download and adapt.
approaches.avoidWhen: You skip checking licenses and quality.

approaches.name: Hosted model APIs
approaches.what: Call a model over the internet.
approaches.greatWhen: Language and vision features with no infrastructure.
approaches.avoidWhen: Strict data rules or huge volume.
approaches.example: Call an API to draft replies.

approaches.name: Hardware: laptop, rented GPU, own servers
approaches.greatWhen: A laptop for small tables, a rented GPU for training, and your own servers when data rules or volume demand it.
approaches.avoidWhen: Buying GPUs before you know you need them.
approaches.example: Rent a GPU for one afternoon to fine-tune.

approaches.name: Version control and reproducibility
approaches.what: Keep code, data versions and settings so results can be repeated.
approaches.example: Keep code in Git and note which data snapshot trained each model.

challenge.question: Two people, no infrastructure and a small budget. What is a sensible first setup?

options.text: Notebooks and a classic ML library for tables, a hosted API for language features, rented GPUs only if needed, and version control from day one
options.why: Light, cheap, and every result can be repeated.

options.text: Buy a rack of GPUs first
options.why: You do not yet know what you need to run.

options.text: Build every tool in-house from scratch
options.why: You would spend the budget rebuilding what already exists.
Fine to start, but it will not scale or repeat.

bestCase.title: Start light, rent what you need, and keep work repeatable
bestCase.example: The team explores in notebooks, trains the return model with a classic library on a laptop, calls a hosted API for reply drafting, rents a GPU for one fine-tuning afternoon, and keeps everything in version control with a note of which data snapshot was used.

worstCase.title: Buying big before knowing the need
worstCase.example: The team spends the budget on two GPU servers, then finds the return model trains in a minute on a laptop. Nobody records which data made which model, so a good result cannot be reproduced.

steps.label: Explore in a notebook
steps.goes: Load orders, plot returns, and spot problems.

steps.label: Prepare data
steps.goes: Clean and split it with a table library.

steps.label: Train and score
steps.goes: A classic ML library trains a model on the laptop.

steps.label: Need more power?
steps.goes: Only for deep learning: rent a GPU for a day.
steps.goesWrong: Two GPU servers are bought up front and sit mostly idle.

steps.label: Save and share
steps.goes: Code, settings and the data version go into version control.

steps.label: Hand over to deployment
steps.goes: A teammate can reproduce and run it.

takeaway: Learn the roles, not the brand names: a language, table and model libraries, notebooks, model hubs, rented hardware, and version control.
